statement: In people averaging less than 30 g of ethanol a day, in seven observational studies pooled by one team, drinking heavily on some occasions compared with drinking the same average amount without such occasions is associated with a higher risk of ischaemic heart disease (deaths and new cases combined); no absolute risks are given. Against lifetime abstainers, people without heavy drinking occasions had a pooled relative risk of 0.64 (95% CI as printed 0.53 to 0.71, an interval that does not fit its point estimate on the log scale, so one figure is probably misprinted; editors' calculation) and people with them 1.12 (0.91 to 1.37), that is, no lower risk than lifetime abstainers; the ratio between the two groups was 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25) (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014). The same team's earlier review, cited second-hand, gave 1.45 (1.24 to 1.70) for people with irregular heavy drinking occasions against people who drank without them. The article does not say what counted as a heavy drinking occasion, which seven studies were pooled or how many people and events they included (all only in a supplement not read); all seven adjusted for age and smoking, one author searched for and extracted the studies, and their risk of bias was not assessed. The review of average intake against lifetime abstainers and the GBD 2016 model did not take drinking pattern into account, and genetic variants that lower average intake also lower heavy drinking (odds of binge drinking 0.78, 0.73 to 0.84, in carriers of the ADH1B variant; Holmes et al., 2014), so two critiques argue that the genetic studies may partly reflect heavy drinking days rather than average amount (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014; Mukamal et al., 2020). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: One team pooled seven studies of people who drank under 30 grams of alcohol a day on average. People who never had heavy drinking days had about a third lower heart disease risk than people who had never drunk. People with heavy drinking days had no lower risk. The team's earlier review pointed the same way. The paper does not say what counted as a heavy day or which studies were used, and the review did not rate the studies' quality. Gene studies lower heavy drinking along with the average amount, so critics say they may partly show the effect of heavy days. None of the studies says how many people out of 100 are affected.
population: People who drink, averaging under 30 g of ethanol a day, in seven observational studies of adult population samples (identities, designs and countries only in the supplement), with lifetime abstainers as the reference; and, second-hand, the studies of the same team's 2010 review
exposure: Heavy drinking occasions (episodic heavy drinking) as defined by each study, at an average intake under 30 g/day; the definition is not given in the article
comparator: Drinking the same average amount without heavy drinking occasions; both groups also compared with lifetime abstainers
outcome: Ischaemic heart disease, deaths and new cases combined (ICD-9 410–414, ICD-10 I20–I25)
magnitude: Roerecke & Rehm 2014 (seven studies; against lifetime abstainers; ischaemic heart disease mortality and morbidity combined; most-adjusted estimates, all adjusted for age and smoking): average under 30 g/day without heavy drinking occasions RR 0.64 (0.53–0.71 as printed; geometric midpoint of that interval 0.61, editors' calculation), I² 10%, Egger P = 0.35; with heavy drinking occasions 1.12 (0.91–1.37), I² 0%, Egger P = 0.58; ratio with against without 1.75 (1.36–2.25), equal to 1.12/0.64 (editors' arithmetic), method of its interval not described. Roerecke & Rehm 2010, as cited by Roerecke & Rehm 2012: RR 1.45 (1.24–1.70), drinkers with irregular heavy drinking occasions against drinkers without them. Holmes et al. 2014: ADH1B intake-lowering variant, binge drinking OR 0.78 (0.73–0.84) and 17.2% fewer UK units a week. No absolute risks, numbers of participants or events, or definition of a heavy drinking occasion in the article.

evidence.extracted: Seven studies met the criteria. Against lifetime abstainers, ischaemic heart disease (deaths and new cases combined) in people averaging under 30 g a day without heavy drinking occasions: relative risk 0.64 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.71, printed identically in the abstract and the results); with heavy drinking occasions: 1.12 (0.91 to 1.37). Editors' calculation: the geometric midpoint of 0.53 to 0.71 is 0.61, so the point estimate or one limit is probably misprinted.

evidence.extracted: Relative risk with against without heavy drinking occasions, at the same average intake under 30 g a day: 1.75 (1.36 to 2.25), higher than the 1.45 of the authors' 2010 meta-analysis; the authors read this as the effect of episodic heavy drinking being greatest at low average intake. How the ratio and its interval were obtained is not described; editors' arithmetic: 1.12 divided by 0.64 is 1.75, and the two estimates share lifetime-abstainer reference groups within studies.

evidence.extracted: 56 of 59 approached studies took part: 261,991 participants of European descent (48% women), with 20,259 coronary events. Carriers of the ADH1B rs1229984 A-allele (carriers of one or two copies against GG homozygotes) reported 17.2% fewer UK units a week (95% CI 15.6% to 18.9%; 218,969 people; one UK unit is 7.9 g of ethanol), had lower odds of being in their study's top third of intake (0.70, 0.68 to 0.73) and of binge drinking (0.78, 0.73 to 0.84), and higher odds of reporting abstention (1.27, 1.21 to 1.34).

evidence.locator: Results and discussion › Experimental evidence, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: No long-term randomized studies of alcohol and ischaemic heart disease exist; short-term studies show dose-dependent effects on surrogate markers (higher HDL cholesterol, less platelet activation, lower fibrinogen, anti-inflammatory effects), and HDL cholesterol is also raised by regular heavy drinking and is highest in people with alcohol use disorder. The authors set aside the ADH1B Mendelian randomization study (Holmes et al., 2014), which concluded there was no protective effect, as hard to compare with the epidemiology because the variant was also linked to less binge drinking.

evidence.extracted: Drinking has at least three dimensions (frequency, usual quantity per occasion, binge drinking) that correlate only partly and differ in their cardiovascular effects; genetic variants lower all three, so genetic analyses cannot separate them, and those linking intake-lowering variants to lower cardiovascular risk may be showing the harm of binge drinking. Genotype tests lifelong (and parental) rather than adult exposure; given common heavy drinking in adolescence and early adulthood, its lower prevalence in young adults carrying ALDH2 variants, and the possibility that binge drinking starts atherosclerosis (a mouse study and a vascular-function study are cited), such analyses may partly test teenage and young-adult heavy drinking, with uncertain relevance to limited drinking in mid-life.
evidence.quote: may well be proving the harm of binge drinking

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_roerecke_2014): single-author search and extraction, languages limited to three, no risk-of-bias appraisal of the seven studies, whose identities are only in a supplement; drinking pattern self-reported once.

inconsistency.note: Low heterogeneity (I² 10% and 0%); the team's earlier review points the same way.

indirectness.note: What counted as a heavy drinking occasion is not stated and probably differs between studies; deaths and new cases are combined; only people averaging under 30 g a day; the populations of the seven studies are not described in the article.

imprecision.note: The ratio's interval (1.36 to 2.25) excludes no difference, though one printed interval appears to be misprinted and the method behind the ratio's interval is not described.

publication_bias.note: Egger's test with seven studies has little power; not assessable.

large_effect.note: The ratio of 1.75 is below 2; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; rated down for risk of bias and indirectness: very low. Rated as worded: an association of drinking pattern with ischaemic heart disease at the same average intake. Status replicated by the same team: the 2010 and 2014 reviews are by the same two authors and may share studies (the legend of the pooled figure marks one entry as taken from the 2010 review, by the first reader's account), and the article does not report the direction of each of the seven studies, so they are not counted as independent replications (§6.4). The genetic critiques are cited only for the argument that pattern and amount move together in genetic studies, not as evidence on pattern.
